title: Leaderboards
brief: Players send their score at the end of every match and open the top-100 table all day. Everyone looks at the same top 100, which makes that one answer extremely popular. A tournament final will make it much worse.

clarify.q: How fresh must the top 100 be?
clarify.a: Five seconds behind is fine. Nobody notices.

clarify.q: Does a player need to see their own new score and rank immediately?
clarify.a: Their own score should show within a second or two. Everyone else can wait a few seconds.
Rarely and only for the last minute. A lost score is a very unhappy player.

notes: One score record is about 100 bytes (approx.).

numbers.label: Score submissions per second at peak
All scores in memory
numbers.how: 8 million players × 100 bytes ≈ 0.8 GB, fits in one cache node (approx.)

numbers.label: Share of reads that ask for the top 100
numbers.how: Roughly half of table views are the global top board during the hot-key event (approx.)

hints: Half the players are asking for the exact same page. Do they each need a fresh answer?
A CDN with a very short time to keep answers (5 seconds) turns thousands of identical reads into a few.
CDN with 5 second answers, then servers, then a cache that holds every score, then a key-value store for safety.

editorial.summary: The top board is one hot answer. Keep it for a few seconds at the edge and the flood of readers becomes a trickle. The rest of the work is a fast in-memory table for a player's own rank and a durable store behind it.

designs.name: Five-second edge copy
designs.why: The CDN keeps the top 100 for 5 seconds and collapses misses, so the origin sees one request per edge per 5 seconds. The cache serves personal ranks and the store makes scores safe.

tradeoffs: A five second copy is slightly stale. Players accept that for a global table, and the saving is enormous.
The player's own rank skips the edge copy, so it stays fresh but costs the origin a lookup.
A sorted set in memory ranks fast. A database must scan or index, which is slower under writes.
Writes go to a durable store too, so a cache restart never wipes the scores.
editorial.realWorld: A popular game can see tens of thousands of score writes a second at a season launch. The top-100 view is one of the most cached pages in the product (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Leaderboards: The same request is delivered twice, and a worker can crash after saving it. What uniqueness constraint and transaction would keep one durable result?
correctness.discussion: Choose a stable business operation id and enforce a unique constraint in the authoritative store. Insert the id, apply the change and save its result in one transaction. A retry returns that result. Recording the id before the change can lose work after a crash; recording it afterwards can apply the change twice. If work continues through a queue, commit an outbox entry in the same transaction and deduplicate at each consumer.

fields.label: The server commits a change, then crashes before replying. The client retries. What happens?
options: Commit the operation id, effect and result atomically; return that result on retry
Record the id first, then apply the change in a separate write
fields.explanation: Recording the id separately can either lose an operation or apply it twice. The effect and deduplication result must commit together.

fields.label: The server acknowledges a write just before its storage fails. Which evidence meets the stated recovery point?
options: A queued backup request with no completed durable copy
A measured replication or backup gap of at most 60 seconds, with a tested replay plan
fields.explanation: A scheduled copy is not a completed copy. Match acknowledgement and recovery to the stated loss boundary.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 1,500 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $5,658. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
